title: Website redesign brief: what to prepare before hiring an agency
AI title: Website redesign brief: what to prepare before hiring an agency
excerpt: Prepare a clear website redesign brief covering goals, scope, content, integrations, budget, ownership and launch checks before you hire an agency.
imageAlt: Website redesign planning cover with a wireframe becoming a finished website and the title Plan Before You Hire.
content:
Before asking an agency to redesign your website, prepare a brief that explains the business problem, the people you need to reach, the pages and functions you need, and how you will judge the finished work. Include your content responsibilities, ownership expectations, available budget and launch constraints. You do not need to arrive with a technical specification. You do need enough clarity for agencies to price the same job.

A useful website redesign brief prevents a familiar situation: three attractive proposals that describe three different projects. One includes copywriting, another assumes you will supply it, and a third leaves migration and maintenance unexplained. This guide helps business owners turn a vague request for a better website into a practical starting point for a productive agency conversation.

## Start with what is not working

Describe the problem before prescribing the solution. “The website feels old” may be true, but it does not tell a designer what needs to improve. More useful statements identify an observable difficulty: visitors cannot understand the service range, mobile enquiries are hard to submit, staff cannot update case studies, or important pages no longer reflect the business.

Collect evidence you already have. This might include repeated customer questions, screenshots of a broken form, search queries, enquiry records or comments from the sales team. Separate evidence from assumptions. A fall in enquiries could involve changes in demand, traffic, pricing or follow-up—not just page design.

Choose a small number of priorities. If the main issue is explaining a complex service, a new animation is unlikely to solve it. If the current site works well except for a difficult booking flow, ask whether a focused improvement would be more appropriate than a full rebuild. An agency should be able to discuss that distinction.

## Define the audience and the decision

A website needs to help a particular visitor make progress. Describe your main customer groups and the questions they ask before contacting you. A local wellness business, an international B2B supplier and a digital subscription platform will need different information even if all three want more enquiries.

For each audience, write down the decision you want to support. An international buyer may need to understand delivery capability and communication before booking a call. A local visitor may first need services, location and availability. Avoid trying to give every audience equal priority on every page.

An illustrative audience statement could be: “Our primary visitors are operations managers comparing service providers. They need to understand our scope, relevant experience and onboarding process before requesting a proposal.” This is a planning example, not a claim about a WebMantu client. Replace it with something your team can recognise from real conversations.

## Turn goals into observable actions

“More sales” is a business goal, but it is too broad to act as the only website acceptance criterion. Define which visitor actions the site should make easier: a completed enquiry, a consultation request, a product purchase, a booking or a useful download. Identify the primary action and any supporting actions.

Then distinguish website functionality from commercial outcomes. You can test whether a form reaches the right inbox and displays a confirmation. You cannot fairly promise that a new design will generate a fixed number of qualified buyers without considering traffic quality, pricing and sales follow-up.

Ask how measurement will work. Specify who owns analytics accounts, which events need tracking, and what can be observed when a third-party booking or payment provider is involved. A click on a booking button is not the same as a completed appointment. Keep those differences visible in your reporting plan.

## Inventory the existing site before adding pages

Create a simple list of current pages and mark each one as keep, improve, merge or remove. Add any genuinely necessary new pages. For each page, note its purpose, audience, content owner and main action. This makes page count more meaningful than a proposal that simply promises ten pages.

Identify material worth protecting: useful service explanations, high-value downloads, product data, customer-approved case studies and pages receiving relevant search traffic. Do not delete everything merely because the design is changing. Equally, do not migrate outdated or duplicate material without a reason.

Google recommends creating content that helps the intended audience and offers substantive value, rather than producing material mainly to attract search traffic ([Google Search Central: people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content)). Apply that principle to your brief: each planned page should answer a real buyer question or support a useful task. More pages alone do not make a stronger site.

## Specify functions as journeys, not buzzwords

A brief that lists “AI, CRM, payments and automation” still leaves major questions unanswered. Describe what each function must do from beginning to end. For a contact form, identify the information collected, destination, confirmation state, spam handling and person responsible for responding.

For payments, explain what is being sold, where the customer starts, how a successful or failed transaction is handled, and where staff reconcile records. Do not share secret keys in a planning document. For a multilingual site, identify the languages, translation owner and how updates will remain consistent.

If you want a chatbot, define its boundaries. What questions may it answer? What source material will it use? When should it direct someone to a person? Avoid adding a feature simply because it sounds advanced. Each integration adds implementation, testing and maintenance responsibilities that need to be visible in the scope.

## Agree who supplies content and proof

Content is often the missing dependency in a website schedule. List what already exists, what needs revision and what must be created. Clarify whether the agency is writing copy, editing your draft, migrating existing text, arranging a shoot or only placing supplied material into layouts.

Name a content owner inside your business. That person should coordinate approvals, confirm service descriptions and obtain permission for testimonials, images and client references. An agency can improve presentation, but it cannot responsibly invent your credentials, project results or commercial terms.

Include a practical delivery plan. For example, approve the main service-page structure before writing every related page. Provide originals rather than screenshots of text where possible. Keep images organised by purpose and record usage permissions. A shared folder full of unrelated files is not the same as a content handover ready for production.

## Describe the visual direction without copying

Share a few references and explain what you like about each. You might appreciate a site's navigation, restrained typography or product comparison layout rather than its colours. Tell the agency which qualities matter to your brand: clear, technical, warm, established or premium, for example.

Also state what you do not want. A business may dislike oversized headings, excessive empty space, stock photography presented as real team imagery, or motion that distracts from the main action. These preferences are easier to address before a detailed design is approved.

References should guide the conversation, not become instructions to copy another company's identity. Ask for a mobile interpretation early. A desktop mockup can look impressive while hiding a long, confusing phone journey. Review the hierarchy and task flow, not just the appearance of individual screens.

## Put accessibility and mobile usability in scope

Do not leave accessibility as an undefined final check. Ask the agency to explain the intended standard, testing approach and responsibilities for both design and content. Include keyboard navigation, visible focus, understandable form labels, readable text and meaningful headings in the conversation.

W3C's planning guidance recommends defining accessibility goals, scope and responsibilities, and including accessibility in procurement and acceptance testing ([W3C WAI: planning accessibility](https://www.w3.org/WAI/planning-and-managing/plan/)). It does not mean an automated score alone certifies the whole website or settles every legal obligation.

For mobile review, choose real tasks. Ask someone to understand a service, find relevant proof and submit an enquiry on a phone. Test with a realistic keyboard, smaller viewport and longer content. Check that chat widgets and sticky controls do not cover important fields or buttons. Record what blocks the task rather than relying only on whether the layout looks balanced.

## Set performance expectations that can be tested

“Lightning fast” is a marketing phrase, not an acceptance test. Ask which page templates will be tested, on what devices or network conditions, using which tools, and when results will be reviewed. Be clear about the effect of large videos, third-party widgets and content added later.

Google identifies Core Web Vitals as measures of loading performance, interactivity and visual stability, while noting that good results do not guarantee top rankings ([Google Search Central: Core Web Vitals](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/core-web-vitals)). A brief can request performance testing without treating a single laboratory score as proof of commercial success.

Ask the agency to distinguish lab tests from real-user data. A newly launched site may not have enough field data immediately. Agree what can be tested before launch and what should be monitored afterwards. This creates a more useful expectation than demanding a perfect score without defining the conditions.

## Protect important URLs and search signals

If existing page URLs will change, include migration planning explicitly. Ask for an inventory of old URLs, their intended destinations and a redirect plan. Identify who updates internal links, canonical references and the sitemap, and who checks for broken paths after launch.

Google's site-move guidance recommends mapping old URLs to relevant new ones and testing the new site; it warns against redirecting many unrelated pages to a generic homepage ([Google Search Central: site moves](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/site-move-with-url-changes)). A redesign does not always require changed URLs, so preserve useful paths when there is no reason to alter them.

Do not accept a blanket promise that rankings cannot change. A significant migration may affect discovery and search presentation while systems process the changes. The brief should require a careful process and monitoring, not an impossible guarantee. If search traffic matters to the business, ensure migration is a priced deliverable rather than an assumption.

## Make ownership and handover explicit

Discuss access before the project begins. Clarify who controls the domain, hosting, source repository, analytics, content system and third-party accounts. Your business should understand which accounts it owns and what access the agency needs to deliver and maintain the work.

Ask what is included at handover: source files, design files where agreed, deployment instructions, administrative access, content-editing guidance and a list of subscriptions or licences. Confirm any restrictions on licensed assets or third-party components. Get contract-specific questions reviewed appropriately rather than assuming this checklist is legal advice.

Support also needs boundaries. Distinguish fixing a defect from adding a new feature or changing approved content. Ask about the support period, reporting method, expected response process and ongoing maintenance options. These details help you compare the full project rather than only the initial build price.

## Share a realistic budget and approval process

You do not need to publish your finances to request a proposal, but a working budget range helps an agency suggest a sensible scope. If the range is uncertain, ask for a core version and clearly priced options. Compare like for like: copywriting, migration, integrations, testing and support can materially change the work involved.

Separate one-time development from recurring costs such as hosting, platform plans, premium software and maintenance. Ask which costs are estimates and which depend on usage or external providers. Avoid treating a lower headline figure as the cheaper option before exclusions are understood.

Explain who can approve decisions and how feedback will be consolidated. A clear decision-maker and timely content approval can matter as much as the proposed technical stack. Mention genuine launch constraints, such as an event or contract renewal, and ask which dependencies could affect that date. Do not assume that every requested feature must be ready for the first release.

## A simple brief you can send to an agency

You can begin with the following headings and add short, specific answers:

- **Business and audience:** What you offer, who you serve and who the site should prioritise.
- **Current problems:** Observable issues, with supporting examples where available.
- **Primary action:** What a useful visit should lead to, and how you will measure it.
- **Pages and content:** Existing inventory, proposed changes and content owners.
- **Functions:** Required journeys, integration destinations and operational responsibilities.
- **Design direction:** Brand assets, useful references and mobile priorities.
- **Quality:** Accessibility, usability, performance and migration expectations.
- **Commercial details:** Budget range, recurring-cost questions, timeline and approvals.
- **Ownership and support:** Required access, deliverables, handover and maintenance.

Send the same starting brief to each shortlisted agency. Invite questions and record the answers so all parties are quoting against the same assumptions. If an agency proposes a different approach, ask it to explain the trade-off and show how the revised scope still addresses your priorities.

## Frequently asked questions

### Do I need to choose a framework before hiring an agency?
Not necessarily. Start with content, visitor journeys, integrations and maintenance needs. Ask the agency to justify its recommended tools against those requirements, including who will update the site and what ongoing costs or dependencies the choice creates.

### Is a full redesign always better than smaller improvements?
No. If the main problems are limited to a few journeys or pages, focused work may be appropriate. A rebuild becomes more relevant when structural, content-management or technical limitations prevent the required improvements. Assess the current site before deciding.

### Will a 2,000-word service page improve SEO?
There is no universal target. Google says it does not have a preferred word count in its people-first guidance. Write enough to answer the visitor's questions clearly; do not expand pages with filler simply to meet an assumed ranking threshold.

### How detailed should a first brief be?
Detailed enough to explain the business problem, audience, scope and constraints, but it does not have to replace discovery. Mark unknowns openly. A thoughtful agency should help resolve them rather than treating uncertainty as permission to make invisible assumptions.

## Turn the brief into a better agency conversation

A good brief is not paperwork for its own sake. It helps you discuss the right problem, compare proposals fairly and recognise whether the delivered website matches what your business needs. Start with priorities, make responsibilities visible and treat the launch as the beginning of ongoing ownership rather than the end of the relationship.
